expression_path_evidence.fact: String.toList calls Internal.toArray, which obtains an Array Char through toByteArray.utf8Decode?.get. The byte-equality statement avoids this Lean UTF-8 decoder.
String.ofList stores List.utf8Encode; the latter is flatMap utf8EncodeChar followed by List.toByteArray.

List.toByteArray uses an accumulator push loop; Array.push models a push with List.concat. This exposes a repeated growing-prefix construction pattern. Its precise share of either observed timeout has not been profiled.
List.data_toByteArray rewrites the data of that loop result to the original byte list.toArray; the generic proof is reusable without replaying a closed loop in the proof body.
Array is a wrapper around a List and List.toArray is Array.mk.
Reducing a projection of a String literal first calls whnf(string_lit_to_constructor(c)).

Literal expansion uses native utf8_decode only to emit a List Char expression made of List.cons (Char.ofNat natLiteral), then applies String.ofList. It does not directly emit a stored ByteArray expression.

The special literal/ String.ofList comparison is late in is_def_eq_core, after lazy delta reduction and structure eta; it also whnf-reduces the constructed literal. It is not evidence of an unconditional early shortcut.

When both sides have the same regular definition head, the kernel tries comparing their arguments before unfolding. Preserving matching utf8Encode heads could permit comparison of character lists, but success and resource use for this closed input are untested.

The unchanged char loader uses the official ToExpr instances: Char is Char.ofNat with raw Nat literal, and List uses List.nil/List.cons. These are the same expression constructor shapes used by kernel literal expansion; this is a source-level compatibility fact, not a new checked input identity.
